text.p: President Bill Clinton will lead efforts to "recreate" NATO at a Madrid summit next week but will resist pressure to invite more than three nations to join the alliance, administration officials said on Wednesday.

Clinton, who departs late on Friday for Spain, has already declared publicly that he wants NATO to extend membership only to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in the hope that would quiet efforts to admit additional members.
France and Italy have been pressing the alliance also to invite Romania and Slovenia during its July 8-9 summit.
"The answer is not no, but no at this time," White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger said when reporters asked about the U.S. attitude toward admitting Romania and Slovenia.
"I would think there'd be some lively discussion of this (at the summit) but at the end of the day ... I think it's fair to say that there will be a consensus on the three."

Berger and Defence Secretary William Cohen, who also discussed the upcoming summit, were cool to calls for the 16-member alliance to commit to including Romania and Slovenia in the "next wave" of countries invited for membership.

"I have met on several occasions now with the leadership of both Romania and Slovenia and encouraged them to continue the path that they have been on," Cohen said, adding that the alliance "will enhance our relationship" with the two through the Partnership for Peace programme, which those who want membership must join.

"We really can't say who is in and who's out because if you start to define that you are excluding other countries," Cohen said. "So what we will do is indicate that the process is open ... We still will have a very strong relationship with them and other countries."

Discussing the overall summit, Berger said Clinton's view "is that America must remain anchored in Europe, that NATO was the most important vehicle of that anchoring." He said Clinton wanted to "recreate and adapt NATO for a new era in order for it to be relevant for the American people and relevant for the security threats that we faced."

Russian objections to NATO expansion will play a minimal role at the summit, which Russian President Boris Yeltsin declined to attend. His absence signals that Russia still opposes its former Cold War foe's expansion into former communist eastern Europe and reserves the right to resist any future waves of enlargement.

Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton fly first to Majorca as the guests of King Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofia and will stay at a Moorish castle. They will go to Madrid on Monday for the two-day summit, which opens the next day.
Clinton planned to visit Poland on Thursday and Romania on Friday before going to Denmark for a state visit.
